analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal aid to career-college programs that leave graduates with heavy debt and low pay, and cancels loans for defrauded students.
analysis.headline: Introduced with six House sponsors in April 2025, the bill has sat in two House committees without a hearing or vote since its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill writes tough federal standards for career and for-profit colleges into law: programs whose graduates end up with heavy loan payments relative to their pay would lose federal student aid, and students misled by a school's false claims could get their loans canceled. It would also stop schools from forcing students into arbitration, stop schools from withholding transcripts over unpaid bills, require schools to spend at least 30% of tuition revenue on actual instruction, and set up a federal enforcement unit and complaint-tracking system to police colleges, loan servicers, and companies that recruit for schools [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Students and former students at career-oriented and for-profit schools gain the most: borrowers misled by a school's false claims would have their federal loans canceled, borrowers stranded by a school's sudden closure would get automatic discharges without applying, and students could no longer be forced into arbitration or have transcripts held over an unpaid balance [S3]. Prospective students would see published debt-to-earnings and earnings figures for every career program and mandatory warnings about failing programs before enrolling [S3]. Taxpayers benefit indirectly, since federal aid would stop flowing to programs that consistently leave graduates unable to repay their loans [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student borrowers and for-profit college students

how_it_helps.text: A program fails the debt test if annual loan payments are 20% or more of discretionary earnings (and 8% of total earnings), and it fails the earnings test if graduates earn no more than a high school graduate in the same state; failing two out of three years cuts off all federal student aid to the program.

Borrowers misled by a school's false claims, aggressive recruiting, or contract breaches would get their federal loans discharged, with past payments refunded, credit reports corrected, and widespread misrepresentation handled as a group discharge without individual applications.

Students at schools that closed would get automatic loan discharges without applying, with the 180-day eligibility window extendable when a school was on probation or under regulatory sanction before closing.

Colleges could no longer force students to arbitrate disputes or bar class actions, and could not withhold a student's official transcript over an unpaid balance — a practice that blocks former students from transferring or proving credentials to employers.
Students would see each career program's published debt-to-earnings and earnings figures and would have to acknowledge warnings before enrolling in a failing program.

A permanent enforcement unit inside the Office of Federal Student Aid would investigate complaints, conduct 'secret shopper' checks on recruiting practices, and raise the cap on civil penalties for each misrepresentation from $25,000 to $100,000 or a share of federal funds received.

A multi-agency committee (Education, Justice, FTC, SEC, Consumer Bureau, Defense, Veterans Affairs, Labor, IRS) would coordinate oversight of for-profit colleges, and a centralized complaint system would track and publicly report complaints against schools and servicers.

Executives and owners of schools that committed fraud or lost federal funds could be barred from running or contracting with other federally aided institutions, and owners would have to personally sign agreements to repay liabilities assessed against their schools.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit colleges and other career education programs would bear the main cost: programs whose graduates carry heavy debt or earn no more than high school graduates would lose federal student aid, misrepresenting schools could face civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation plus student lawsuits, and school owners would have to sign personal agreements to repay liabilities assessed by the Department [S3]. Institutions would also have to spend at least 30% of tuition and fee revenue on instruction and report marketing and recruiting spending separately [S3]. Loan servicers and third-party servicers would face an enforcement unit, a complaint system, and contract penalties [S3]. The bill also makes federal administrative funds (capped at 5% of the outstanding loan portfolio) available outside the normal annual appropriations process to run these oversight functions [S3].

drawbacks.text: The 30% instruction-spending requirement applies to all colleges receiving federal aid, and compliance definitions (what counts as 'instruction' versus marketing) could impose reporting burdens on schools that already spend most tuition on teaching while doing little to change bad actors.

The bill makes up to 5% of the outstanding student loan portfolio — tens of billions of dollars — available for administrative costs without an annual appropriation, reducing Congress's regular budget control over Education Department spending.

Codifying broad borrower defense discharge shifts the cost of forgiving loans from defrauded borrowers to taxpayers, and the bill's instruction that the Secretary draw 'all inferences and presumptions' for borrowers could sweep in claims beyond clear-cut fraud.

The three-year ban on reestablishing a failed program could push marginal schools toward closure rather than improvement, leaving enrolled students mid-program when a school shuts down — precisely the harm the closed school discharge provision then has to clean up.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students defrauded by predatory schools and taxpayers who fund their loans, the bill's protections are substantial and targeted: aid stops flowing to programs that consistently fail a measurable earnings-and-debt standard, and defrauded borrowers get a statutory path to discharge. The costs fall almost entirely on the for-profit college sector and loan servicers, which is the point of the bill. The main honest concerns are design issues, not the core aim: the instruction-spending floor and the automatic administrative funding pot are broad instruments that add compliance work for well-behaved colleges and loosen annual budget control, and broad borrower-defense language could cost taxpayers more than a narrower rule would. The bill has received no committee action, so none of these tradeoffs have been tested in debate or amendment.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce and Judiciary Committees in April 2025 and has sat there without a hearing or vote ever since.

narrative.text: Representative Mark Takano introduced the bill on April 10, 2025, with five Democratic cosponsors, and the Speaker's referral sent it to both the Education and Workforce Committee and the Judiciary Committee.
The only action since introduction is the committee referral; no hearing, markup, or vote has taken place.

The bill would convert several Obama-era Education Department rules — gainful employment, borrower defense to repayment, and closed school discharges — from regulation into statute, which matters because later administrations can rewrite or rescind regulations but cannot change statutes without Congress.
With 5 Democratic cosponsors out of 217 House Democrats and no Republican sponsorship on the public record, the bill has little visible support in a chamber where Republicans hold 223 of 440 seats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges, third-party servicers, and loan servicers are better off so far, because the accountability rules in the bill have not advanced and current looser oversight remains in place. Students and borrowers gain nothing yet.

for.name: Rep. Mark Takano

against.name: Rep. Tim Walberg

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 10, 2025; no hearing or markup on the bill has been scheduled since.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 10, 2025; no action on the bill since.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against gainful employment rules, borrower defense regulations, and similar accountability measures in prior years; the bill would codify several of them into statute.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; the only visible support is six House Democrats, with no Republicans sponsoring and the Republican-led committees not acting on the bill.

industries.industry: For-profit colleges and career education programs
industries.note: The bill's centerpiece targets schools whose graduates cannot repay their loans: failing career programs would lose federal aid for at least three years, misrepresentations would trigger six-figure penalties and student lawsuits, and executives of shuttered schools could be barred from running new ones. Federal student aid is the lifeblood of this sector, so the financial stakes are large.

industries.industry: Third-party servicers and student loan servicers
industries.note: These companies — which run recruiting, marketing, and instructional services for colleges and handle federal loan billing — would face expanded federal oversight, a mandatory complaint system, civil penalties scaled to their contract size, and liability in student lawsuits for misrepresentations.
The accreditation gatekeepers of federal aid would face new duties to assess and monitor the risk schools pose to students, with the threat of losing federal recognition if they do not.

The 30%-of-tuition instruction spending floor and separate marketing/recruitment reporting apply to all institutions receiving federal aid, not just for-profit schools, though well-resourced nonprofit and public universities already typically clear the spending threshold.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 223 House seats and all bill sponsors being Democrats, the bill would need the House Education and Workforce Committee to schedule a hearing or markup, which has not happened since the April 2025 referral. Most bills at this stage with no committee action and no crossover sponsorship do not advance; unless the committee acts or provisions are attached to a larger higher education reauthorization, the bill is likely to sit in committee for the rest of the Congress [S1][S5].
